input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-344: Programming Language Concepts. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course is a study of the syntax and semantics of a diverse set of high-level programming languages. The languages chosen are compared and contrasted in order to demonstrate general principles of programming language design and implementation. The course emphasizes the concepts underpinning modern languages rather than the mastery of particular language details. Programming projects will be required. Prerequisites: CSCI-243 or SWEN-250 or IGME-309 or 4003-334 or 4010-361 or 4080-487) and (MATH-190 or MATH-200) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

Source excerpts:

[acm-code-of-ethics]
The ACM Code directs computing professionals to contribute to society and human well-being. Computing professionals should avoid harm. They should be honest and trustworthy. They should be fair and take action not to discriminate. They should respect the work required to produce new ideas and creative works. They should respect privacy. They should honor confidentiality. Professionals should strive to achieve high quality in both processes and products. They should maintain high standards of professional competence, conduct, and ethical practice. Robust security should be designed and implemented when appropriate. Ethical computing decisions identify stakeholders, foreseeable benefits and harms, uncertainty, alternatives, and obligations.

[acm-research-practice]
Responsible technical communication distinguishes claims from evidence. It cites prior work and identifies the contribution being reported. Methods should be described well enough for readers to evaluate the work. Results should be reported accurately rather than selected to create a misleading conclusion. Limitations and threats to validity should be made visible. Authors should preserve research integrity and avoid plagiarism, fabrication, and falsification. Conflicts and relevant relationships should be disclosed according to publication policy. A research project narrows a question, reviews literature, defines a reproducible method, evaluates results, and communicates for the intended audience.

[rit-csci-344]
This course is a study of the syntax and semantics of a diverse set of high-level programming languages. The languages chosen are compared and contrasted in order to demonstrate general principles of programming language design and implementation. The course emphasizes the concepts underpinning modern languages rather than the mastery of particular language details. Programming projects will be required. Prerequisites: CSCI-243 or SWEN-250 or IGME-309 or 4003-334 or 4010-361 or 4080-487) and (MATH-190 or MATH-200) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

beats.claim: CSCI-344 focuses on the syntax and semantics of a diverse set of high-level programming languages rather than mastery of particular language details.
beats.example: Students will examine how Python and Java handle variable declaration and type checking to see how syntax rules differ while serving the same semantic purpose.
beats.title: Introduction to Course Scope and Objectives
beats.visualDirection: Display a side-by-side comparison chart of Python and Java variable declarations with callouts highlighting syntax differences and shared semantic goals.

beats.claim: Syntax refers to the formal rules that determine the correct structure of statements and expressions in a programming language.
beats.example: In C++, a missing semicolon at the end of a statement causes a compilation error, demonstrating how syntax rules enforce code structure.
beats.title: Defining Syntax in Programming Languages
beats.visualDirection: Show a code snippet with a syntax error highlighted in red, alongside the corrected version with a green checkmark and a brief annotation explaining the rule.

beats.claim: Semantics defines the meaning of valid syntax, including how expressions are evaluated and how programs interact with their environment.
beats.example: The expression `x = 5 + 3` has the same syntactic structure in multiple languages, but its semantic evaluation depends on the language's operator precedence and variable scoping rules.
beats.title: Defining Semantics in Programming Languages
beats.visualDirection: Display a flowchart showing the evaluation steps of a simple arithmetic expression, with nodes labeled by language-specific semantic rules.

beats.claim: Different programming languages use distinct syntax conventions to represent the same conceptual operations, reflecting varied design philosophies.
beats.example: Python uses indentation to define code blocks, while C# uses curly braces, demonstrating how syntax choices impact readability and structure.
beats.title: Comparing Syntax Across Languages
beats.visualDirection: Show two code blocks side-by-side, one in Python and one in C#, with arrows pointing to the structural delimiters and a caption explaining the syntactic difference.

beats.claim: Semantic rules govern how languages interpret code, including type systems, memory management, and execution models, which directly affect program behavior.
beats.example: JavaScript uses dynamic typing where variable types are determined at runtime, whereas Java uses static typing where types are checked at compile time, illustrating different semantic approaches to data handling.
beats.title: Comparing Semantics Across Languages
beats.visualDirection: Create a table comparing dynamic vs. static typing with columns for type checking time, error detection, and flexibility, using JavaScript and Java as examples.

beats.claim: Modern programming languages share underlying design principles such as modularity, abstraction, and consistency, which simplify learning and implementation.
beats.example: Both Python and C# support object-oriented programming through classes and inheritance, demonstrating how abstraction principles are implemented across different syntaxes.
beats.title: Identifying General Principles of Language Design
beats.visualDirection: Display a diagram of a class hierarchy with inheritance arrows, labeled with common OOP concepts, and a note explaining how these principles appear in multiple languages.

beats.claim: Students can analyze a programming language feature by breaking it down into syntactic rules, semantic interpretations, and design principles to solve implementation challenges.
beats.example: When debugging a loop in a new language, students first verify syntax correctness, then trace semantic execution flow, and finally check for design principle violations like infinite recursion.
beats.title: Applying Problem-Solving Methods to Language Analysis
beats.visualDirection: Show a three-step checklist graphic: 1) Check syntax, 2) Trace semantics, 3) Verify design principles, with each step containing a brief actionable prompt.

beats.claim: Programming projects are required to reinforce the application of syntax, semantics, and design principles through hands-on implementation and comparison.
beats.example: Students will write a small utility in two different languages, then document how syntax and semantic differences affected the implementation and final output.
beats.title: Connecting to Course Requirements and Projects
beats.visualDirection: Display a project workflow diagram showing language selection, coding, testing, and documentation phases, with callouts linking each phase to core course concepts.

beats.claim: Understanding syntax and semantics enables programmers to navigate diverse languages, apply general design principles, and approach new programming challenges systematically.
beats.example: When encountering an unfamiliar language, programmers can quickly identify syntax patterns, predict semantic behavior, and leverage shared design principles to accelerate learning.
beats.title: Reviewing Key Takeaways and Next Steps
beats.visualDirection: Show a summary slide with three icons representing syntax, semantics, and design principles, each with a concise bullet point reinforcing the core lesson.

beats.claim: A structured checklist ensures thorough evaluation of programming language features by verifying syntax validity, semantic accuracy, and alignment with design principles.
beats.example: Before submitting a code snippet, students check for correct syntax, trace semantic execution paths, and confirm that the implementation follows modular and consistent design practices.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Display a printable checklist template with three columns: Syntax Verification, Semantic Trace, and Design Principle Alignment, each with checkboxes and brief instructions.

learningObjectives: Define and distinguish between syntax and semantics in high-level programming languages.
Compare and contrast at least two programming languages to identify general principles of language design and implementation.
Apply a structured problem-solving method to analyze a programming language feature using the course's core concepts.
